newsitem.title: FRANCE: Study on French car industry due end January.
newsitem.headline: Study on French car industry due end January.

text.p: A government-commissioned study on whether the French car industry needs to cut workers to survive should be completed around the end of the month, an Industry Ministry official said on Wednesday.

Industry Minister Franck Borotra retained expert Bernard Cabaret in November to conduct the study after carmakers Renault and PSA Peugeot Citroen sought the government's help and approval to carry out mass early retirement programmes.

The ministry official said Cabaret had been asked to address three issues -- whether staff reductions are essential to the industry, whether they will be enough to ensure its survival, and, if cuts are necessary, the best way to carry them out.
The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said Cabaret had interviewed managers not only at the French car companies but also at other European carmakers.
The European car industry faces stiffer competition from the year 2000 when import barriers are removed and is also plagued by overcapacity, Borotra said at a New Year's reception for the press.
The official said both Borotra and Prime Minister Alain Juppe had made it clear that a solution would have to be "give-and-take", requiring sacrifices from both the companies and the staffs.

The ministry and the two companies have never confirmed the number of staff cuts sought, but French newspapers reported a figure of around 40,000, which would represent about 15 percent of the combined staffs of the two companies.
Last month PSA Peugeot Citroen chairman Jacques Calvet said the company might have to lay off workers if the government did not agree to the early retirement proposal.
The companies are asking the government to finance a bigger share of early retirement costs to avoid outright layoffs.
Borotra said the car industry would be one of the ministry's priorities in 1997.
But he said it was essential to tackle France's big jobless rate, and youth unemployment, in particular. "Companies cannot prosper in a miserable environment," he said.
